title: Radical Acceptance
sources: Full text of Radical Acceptance (Bantam 2004 printing of the 2003 book), read from the archive.org copy: prologue, chapter 1 (The Trance of Unworthiness), chapter 3 (The Sacred Pause), chapter 4 (Unconditional Friendliness), chapter 5 (Coming Home to Our Body)

facts.claim: Prologue: in college Brach spent a weekend hiking in the mountains with an older, wiser friend of twenty-two. Sitting by a stream, the friend described learning to be 'her own best friend'; a wave of sadness came over Brach and she broke down sobbing.

In her early teens Brach sometimes imagined living inside a transparent orb that separated her from people and life around her; when she felt bad about herself the walls were thick, when she felt good the bubble thinned to an invisible wisp.

Brach describes herself then as harassed by an inner judge, 'merciless, relentless, nit-picking, driving, often invisible but always on the job'. Her guiding assumption was 'Something is fundamentally wrong with me'. In the eyes of the world she was highly functional; internally she was anxious, driven and often depressed.

A meditation student, Marilyn, had spent many hours at the bedside of her dying mother: reading to her, meditating beside her late at night, holding her hand. One morning before dawn the mother, mostly unconscious, opened her eyes, looked intently at her daughter and whispered, 'You know, all my life I thought something was wrong with me.' She shook her head slightly, closed her eyes, drifted back into a coma and died several hours later.
Marilyn called it her mother's 'parting gift': she realised she did not have to lose her life the same way, and resolved to hold herself with more acceptance and kindness.

Brach coins 'the trance of unworthiness': living through a lens of personal insufficiency, unable to see who we really are. She has worked twenty years as psychologist and Buddhist teacher with thousands of clients and students; at a ten-day retreat or in a weekly therapy session the suffering, the fear of being flawed and unworthy, is basically the same.

It takes little to set it off: hearing of someone else's accomplishments, being criticised, an argument, a mistake at work. A friend put it: 'Feeling that something is wrong with me is the invisible and toxic gas I am always breathing.'

Brach's recurring dream: running up a hill, climbing boulders or swimming against a current, a loved one in trouble, mind speeding but body heavy 'as if through molasses', sure she should be able to handle it. She says it captures the essence of the trance.
In the trance we replay worries while eating lunch, driving home from work, talking to partners or reading to children at night; inherent in it is the belief that we are always falling short.
The trance does not always look like shame. A successful writer and teacher friend told her 'My main challenge isn't shame, it's pride', describing how easily she feels superior to others.

One of Brach's therapy clients has a thirteen-year-old son diagnosed with attention deficit disorder; despite doctors, diet, acupuncture, drugs and love, he struggles and feels isolated, and she lives in anguish feeling she is failing him.

Chapter 5: Brach and her husband planned a home birth, without drugs, with a midwife. She wanted to be as wakeful and present as possible and trusted her meditation and yoga practice to help her 'go with the flow'.
Early in labor, knowing that resisting contractions only made them worse, she relaxed with them, breathing, making sounds without inhibition, 'riding the pain as a natural part of the process'.

When her son's head started crowning the pain level shot up. She thought 'This much pain has got to mean something is going wrong'. Her whole body tightened and her deep slow breaths turned into the shallow, quick breathing of panic; her confidence and resolve were gone.

Her midwife, used to seeing fear and resistance in response to pain, said 'Nothing's wrong, honey . . . it's all completely natural, it's just painful.' She had to say it several times before it began to sink in; then, in the middle of burning pain, explosive pressure, tearing and exhaustion, Brach remembered to breathe deeply and relax. 'It was just pain, not wrong.'

Brach's reading: when she reacted with fear she added to the unpleasant sensations the belief that something was wrong. 'The Buddha taught that we suffer when we cling to or resist experience'; she cites the saying 'Pain is inevitable, but suffering is optional'. She adds that the fear of pain is often the most unpleasant part of a painful experience.

For four years Brach struggled with chronic illness. Each bout of fatigue or indigestion flooded her mind with stories ('Something's very wrong . . . maybe I'm seriously sick', 'I pushed too hard and didn't get enough sleep', 'I've been drinking too much black tea, the acid must have affected my stomach'); with a stomach cramp came a feeling of personal weakness and shame. She wonders whether the judgments and worries that tightened her muscles against the pain increased her exhaustion.

She quotes Jon Kabat-Zinn: symptoms and your feelings about them are messengers; in the old days a king who disliked the message might have the messenger killed; 'killing the messenger and denying the message or raging against it' is not an intelligent way to approach healing. Pain is the body's call to pay attention: burning heat, we pull our hand from the fire; weakness and headache, we eat something.

Chapter 5, anger: halfway through son Narayan's eighth-grade year, he and Brach were in a painful, angry standoff; his grades were sliding and they fought daily over rules about computer play, homework, phone time and bedtime. The more she monitored, reminded and scolded, the more he turned a deaf ear. His room had become a late-night video arcade.

Her anger seeped into daily life: she sat in the car stewing if he kept her waiting; pounced when he forgot to feed the dog or change the cat litter; when he asked her to order a pizza she answered vindictively, 'Well, you didn't clean your room, so why should I?'

Lying awake one night she imagined looking back on his teen years and seeing that misunderstandings and anger had devoured their time together. The pain of this jarred her. She had forgotten to apply the pause she regularly used, and resolved to pause before the next encounter.

The next evening, half an hour past the agreed homework time, she stood outside his closed door and heard the muffled sounds of Everquest, his favourite computer game. Anger rose; she imagined heaving a giant boulder into the screen, a recurring fantasy. Instead she waited.

In the pause she noticed her body: the anger felt like mounting pressure in chest and throat, tight shoulders and hands, clenched jaw, pounding heart, heat in her face. She says it would have been far easier to barge in.

The sensations shifted. The pressure gave way to a deep soreness 'as if a fist were gripping my heart'. 'I'm afraid of something,' she realised: afraid Narayan would fail in life and be unhappy, and that it was all her fault. When a blame story ('It's his fault I feel like this') almost sent her through the door she returned her attention to her body. Then a sinking feeling, a heavy ache, and moist eyes; the stories of blame and failure receded and a tenderness grew.

She knocked; he mumbled 'C'min'. He looked up with guilty eyes: 'I was just getting off, Mom. What time is it anyway?' (his watch was on the dresser, not his wrist). He asked 'Are you angry? I'm sorry . . . I just lost track.' She pulled a chair close and said 'It's okay, hon, but we need to talk.'

What she said about study habits and agreements was not new, but she felt different: aware of her breath, her posture, where her hands rested, how her face tightened. When he spoke she listened, heard how much he got from mastering the game, and could sympathise with 'lights out' when he was not tired. When she kissed the top of his head and left there was 'a good warm feeling between us'.

Brach's reading: by opening to the sensations she discovered the roots of her reactivity; she had been avoiding the unpleasant sensations that make up fear and sorrow. 'By opening mindfully to the play of sensations, the grip of my anger and stories naturally loosened.'

rejected.claim: Brach's patient with chronic back pain asks 'why me, this is unfair' (story 1558 old text)
rejected.reason: Not found in the full text. The book's pain story is Brach's own labor and her four-year chronic illness; a friend's disc injury is the only back-related case.

rejected.claim: The 'second arrow' teaching used as Brach's framework for primary versus secondary suffering
rejected.reason: The phrase 'two arrows' / 'second arrow' does not appear in the book. Book's own formulation: 'Pain is inevitable, but suffering is optional'.

rejected.claim: Brach asks retreat audiences 'who feels something is wrong with me?' and most hands go up; 'yetersizlik transi' as survey finding (1559 old text)
rejected.reason: No hand-raising scene in the text. The book's own evidence is Brach's story, Marilyn's mother, clients.

rejected.claim: Evolutionary and cultural twin origin of the unworthiness feeling as stated by Brach (1559 old text)
rejected.reason: Not stated in that form for unworthiness; evolution is discussed for pain and fear. Dropped.

rejected.claim: 'Becoming aware of the feeling makes a door open so that I am not this feeling' (1559 old text)
rejected.reason: Not a quoted statement of the book.

rejected.claim: RAIN (Recognize, Allow, Investigate, Nurture) taught to a client who arrives angry to every meeting; anger sits over fear, over sadness, over loneliness (1560 old text)
rejected.reason: RAIN is not named in this book; the 'Nurture' version is from Brach's later work. The client case is not in the text. Anger-to-fear-to-grief sequence IS present in Brach's own Narayan story and is used instead.

rejected.claim: 'Emotions do not pass because they are not seen' as Brach's quote

1558.note: Rebuilt around Brach's labor and the midwife's line; the patient and 'second arrow' framing are not in the book. Book's own saying about pain and suffering used.

1559.note: Rebuilt around Marilyn's dying mother and Brach's own prologue; hand-raising scene and evolutionary claims dropped.

1560.note: RAIN is not in this book; rebuilt around Brach's anger at her son, which carries the same anger-to-fear-to-grief insight from the book itself.
